title: How to Price Your Products Correctly
summary: Most Cameroonian SME owners price by guessing or copying competitors. Here is a simple system that ensures every sale makes you money.
author: BizNess Editorial
content:
# How to Price Your Products Correctly

One of the most common reasons small businesses fail in Cameroon is simple: the owner is charging too little. Not because they are lazy or careless — but because nobody ever taught them how to calculate a proper price. This article will fix that.

## The Three Numbers You Must Know Before Setting Any Price

Before you put a price on anything, you need to know three things:

**1. Your Cost Price (What it costs YOU to get or make the item)**
This is everything you spend to have the product ready to sell. If you buy rice to resell, it is the price you paid the wholesaler plus transport cost to bring it to your shop. If you make food, it is the cost of all ingredients plus the gas or charcoal you used to cook it.

Most owners forget half their costs. They remember the main ingredient but forget: packaging, transport, the electricity to run the fridge, the gas for the motorbike, the time spent going to the market. All of these are real costs.

**2. Your Overhead (The cost of keeping your business alive)**
Every month you pay rent, possibly phone credit for customer communication, soap to keep the shop clean, airtime to call suppliers. These costs exist even on days you sell nothing. You must share these costs across everything you sell.

Simple formula: Add up all your monthly overhead costs and divide by the number of items you typically sell in a month. That gives you your overhead cost per item.

Example: You pay 30,000 CFA rent and 5,000 CFA in other fixed costs monthly. You sell roughly 350 items per month. Overhead per item = 35,000 ÷ 350 = 100 CFA per item.

**3. Your Profit Margin (What you actually want to earn)**
This is not a dirty word. You deserve to earn for your time and risk. A healthy margin for most Cameroonian retail businesses is between 20% and 40% on top of total costs.

## The Pricing Formula

**Selling Price = (Cost Price + Overhead per Item) × (1 + Profit Margin %)**

Example: A bag of rice costs you 4,500 CFA from the wholesaler. Overhead per bag is 150 CFA. You want a 25% margin.

Total cost = 4,500 + 150 = 4,650 CFA
Selling price = 4,650 × 1.25 = **5,812 CFA** (round to 5,800 or 6,000 CFA)

## Why Copying Your Competitor's Price Is Dangerous

Your competitor may pay less for stock because they buy in larger quantities. Their rent may be lower. They may be losing money on that item and making it up elsewhere. You have no idea what their costs are. Their price tells you nothing useful about what YOU should charge.

The right question is never 'what is my competitor charging?' The right question is 'what do I need to charge to survive and grow?'

## What to Do When Customers Say Your Price Is Too High

First, stay calm. 'Too expensive' is the most common thing customers say in any market, anywhere in the world — it is part of negotiation culture, not a statement of fact.

Second, know your floor. Before any negotiation, know the minimum price that still covers all your costs and a small profit. Never go below that number, no matter what. Selling below cost is not a sale — it is paying a customer to take your goods.

Third, explain your value. If your palm oil is fresh-pressed and better quality, say so. If you offer credit and your competitor does not, that is worth something.

## Action: Do This Today

Pick your three best-selling products. Calculate the true cost price for each one, including all hidden costs. Calculate your overhead share per item. Then check whether your current selling price gives you at least a 20% margin. You may be surprised — and concerned — by what you find.

title: Cash Flow vs Profit — Why You Can Go Broke While Making Money
summary: Many business owners are shocked when their business collapses despite making sales every day. Cash flow is why. Understanding this difference can save your business.
author: BizNess Editorial
content:
# Cash Flow vs Profit — Why You Can Go Broke While Making Money

Here is a story that happens across Cameroon every week. A business owner is selling well, customers are happy, the books say profit — and then one morning they cannot pay their supplier, cannot pay rent, cannot make change for a customer. The business collapses. Neighbours say the owner was careless. The real reason is something almost nobody explains: the difference between profit and cash flow.

## What Is Profit?

Profit is simple. It is what is left after you subtract your costs from your revenue.

Revenue: 500,000 CFA
Costs: 380,000 CFA
Profit: 120,000 CFA

This looks healthy. You made money. So why are you broke?

## What Is Cash Flow?

Cash flow is about TIMING. It is whether you have actual money in your hand right now to pay what you owe right now.

You can be profitable and still have zero cash. Here is how:

- You sold 200,000 CFA worth of goods to a contractor who will pay you next month
- You gave 150,000 CFA worth of stock to regular customers on credit
- You paid your supplier 180,000 CFA for new stock today

On paper, you have 120,000 CFA profit. In your pocket, you have nothing — and your rent is due tomorrow.

This is a cash flow crisis. It has nothing to do with whether your business is profitable or not.

## The Three Most Common Cash Flow Killers in Cameroonian SMEs

**1. Too much credit given to customers**
Credit culture is deeply embedded in Cameroonian commerce. Customers expect it. But every CFA you are owed by a customer is a CFA you cannot use to pay your rent, restock, or handle an emergency. Many businesses collapse not from lack of sales but from too much unpaid debt sitting on the customer side.

**2. Paying suppliers before collecting from customers**
You buy stock on cash terms but sell on credit. The gap between paying out and receiving back is when businesses suffocate.

**3. Big expenses arriving together**
Rent, school fees, supplier payment, and equipment repair all fall in the same week. Each one alone is manageable. Together they drain every CFA you have.

## How to Protect Your Cash Flow

**Set a strict credit limit per customer.** Know the maximum you will allow any single customer to owe you. When they reach it, stop giving credit until they pay. Be firm. A lost sale is better than a lost business.

**Collect before you restock.** Before you make a major supplier payment, spend two days recovering outstanding debts. Turn those receivables into cash first.

**Keep a 'survival fund.'** Set aside a percentage of every single day's income — even 5% — into a separate account or envelope that you do not touch unless the business is about to stop operating. One month's operating costs is the target.

**Map your cash calendar.** Write down every expense you know is coming in the next 30 days and the date it is due. Write down every payment you expect to receive and when. Compare them. If outgoing arrives before incoming, you have a cash flow problem forming — and now you have time to fix it before it breaks you.

## The One Question to Ask Every Week

Forget 'did I make profit this week?' Ask instead: **'If every bill I owe arrived tomorrow, could I pay them?'**

If the answer is no, your cash flow needs attention regardless of what your profit looks like.

title: How to Register Your Business Formally in Cameroon (Step by Step)
summary: Operating informally feels easier but it costs you — loans, contracts, and protection are all closed off. Here is exactly how to formalise your business in Cameroon.
author: BizNess Editorial
content:
# How to Register Your Business Formally in Cameroon (Step by Step)

Most small businesses in Cameroon operate informally. Some do so for years, even decades. It feels simpler — no forms, no fees, no bureaucracy. But operating informally has a real cost that becomes visible when it matters most: you cannot open a business bank account, cannot bid on government contracts, cannot access formal loans, and have no legal protection if a client refuses to pay.

This article walks you through how to formally register a business in Cameroon and what it actually gives you.

## The Two Main Business Structures to Consider

**Entreprise Individuelle (Sole Proprietorship)**
The simplest structure. You are the business. Fast to register, low cost, minimal paperwork. Best for: traders, artisans, food sellers, service providers starting out. The downside is that legally your personal assets and business assets are the same — if the business owes money, your personal property can be targeted.

**SARL (Société à Responsabilité Limitée)**
A limited liability company. Your personal assets are protected if the business fails. Requires a minimum capital of 100,000 CFA under OHADA reforms. Best for: any business that deals with significant amounts of money, has employees, or plans to grow. More paperwork but much stronger legal protection.

## Where to Go: The CFCE

Cameroon established the **Centre de Formalités de Création d'Entreprises (CFCE)** specifically to make business registration faster. It is a one-stop shop where you can complete most registration steps in one place instead of visiting five different government offices.

There are CFCE offices in Douala, Yaoundé, Bafoussam, and other regional capitals. This is your starting point.

## Step-by-Step Registration Process

**Step 1: Choose your business name**
Check that the name is not already taken. The CFCE can verify this. You will also need to decide your business activity — what exactly your business does, described in official terms.

**Step 2: Prepare your documents**
For an Entreprise Individuelle you typically need:
- Valid national identity card (CNI)
- Proof of address (utility bill or tenancy agreement)
- Passport photos
- Completed registration form (available at the CFCE)

For a SARL, add:
- Articles of association (statuts), which a notary drafts
- Proof of initial capital deposit at a bank
- Identity documents for all partners/shareholders

**Step 3: Register with the RCCM**
The **Registre du Commerce et du Crédit Mobilier (RCCM)** is the official business register under OHADA law used across 17 African countries including Cameroon. Registration gives you your official business number. The CFCE handles this as part of the one-stop process.

**Step 4: Obtain your Taxpayer Identification Number (NIU)**
The **Numéro d'Identifiant Unique (NIU)** is your tax registration number. Required to issue receipts, open a business bank account, and deal with any government entity. Also handled at the CFCE.

**Step 5: Register with CNPS (if you have employees)**
The **Caisse Nationale de Prévoyance Sociale (CNPS)** is Cameroon's social security agency. If you hire any employee, even one, you are legally required to register them with CNPS and pay social contributions.

## What Does It Cost?

Fees vary by business type and location but expect between 30,000 and 150,000 CFA for a basic Entreprise Individuelle registration including all certificates. A SARL with a notary will cost more — typically 150,000 to 400,000 CFA depending on the notary and complexity.

## What You Get After Registration

- A business bank account (banks require RCCM number and NIU)
- Access to microfinance loans that require formal registration
- Ability to sign formal contracts that are legally enforceable
- Ability to issue official invoices and receipts (factures)
- Eligibility for government procurement and tenders
- Protection under OHADA commercial law

Formalisation does not mean you immediately start paying large taxes. Most small businesses pay a minimum flat-rate tax (impôt libératoire) which is modest. The fear of taxation is usually far larger than the reality for small businesses.

title: Managing Customer Debt — How to Get Paid Without Losing Clients
summary: Giving credit to customers is part of doing business in Cameroon. But uncontrolled credit destroys more businesses than any other single factor. Here is how to manage it properly.
author: BizNess Editorial
content:
# Managing Customer Debt — How to Get Paid Without Losing Clients

In almost every market, kiosk, and small shop across Cameroon, the same conversation happens daily: 'I will pay you at the end of the month.' 'Give it to me today, my salary arrives next week.' 'You know me — I always pay.'

Credit to customers is not going away. It is part of the social fabric of commerce here. The question is not whether to give credit, but how to give it without destroying your business.

Research consistently shows that unrecovered customer debt is one of the top three causes of small business failure in sub-Saharan Africa. Not bad management, not low sales — unpaid debt.

## The Four Rules of Safe Credit

**Rule 1: Know your limit before you say yes**
Before any customer asks for credit, decide in advance: what is the maximum I will allow any single customer to owe me? It might be 5,000 CFA for a casual customer, 20,000 CFA for a regular one you know well. Write it down. When a customer reaches their limit, stop. No exceptions — because the moment you make one exception, the rule no longer exists.

**Rule 2: Write it down every time**
A verbal agreement is forgotten selectively. Keep a credit book — physical or in your app — where every credit transaction is recorded with: customer name, phone number, date, amount, and agreed repayment date. When the customer sees you writing it down, they know you are serious. The act of recording changes the psychology of the transaction.

**Rule 3: Set a repayment date at the moment of credit**
Do not say 'pay whenever you can.' Say 'I will see you on the 15th?' This gives them a target and gives you a date to follow up. Without a specific date, human psychology defaults to 'there is no urgency.'

**Rule 4: Follow up before the date, not after**
Do not wait until after the repayment date to remind a customer. Two days before, send a WhatsApp message: 'Good morning! Just a reminder that your balance of 7,500 CFA is due on Thursday. Thank you as always.' Friendly, firm, specific. This approach recovers significantly more debt than waiting for the date to pass and then chasing.

## How to Recover Debt Without Destroying the Relationship

The fear of 'seeming rude' stops many business owners from collecting what they are owed. But consider this: the customer who has not paid you in three months and keeps buying more on credit is not your friend — they are costing you money every day.

**First reminder:** Friendly, assume it was forgotten. WhatsApp or in-person.

**Second reminder (1 week later):** More direct. 'I wanted to remind you that your balance has been outstanding for three weeks. When can I expect payment?'

**Third reminder (2 weeks later):** Firm. 'I am unable to extend any further credit until your current balance is settled. I appreciate your business and look forward to resolving this.'

**Stop credit immediately.** Do not extend more credit to someone who has not paid existing debt. This seems obvious but it is violated constantly because of social pressure.

## The Customer Who Will Never Pay

Every business owner has at least one. You know who they are. They have excuses for every occasion. The money is always 'coming tomorrow.'

Decide a threshold: if a debt is older than 60 days with no payment and no credible plan, it is almost certainly unrecoverable. Write it off mentally, stop extending credit, and learn the lesson. Chasing it will cost you more in time and stress than the amount is worth.

The most important thing is not recovering that specific debt — it is making sure no other customer reaches that same situation by applying your rules consistently from today forward.

title: Understanding Your Real Costs — You Are Probably Charging Too Little
summary: Fixed costs, variable costs, hidden costs — most SME owners only count half their costs. This guide shows you exactly how to calculate what your business really costs to run.
author: BizNess Editorial
content:
# Understanding Your Real Costs — You Are Probably Charging Too Little

Ask most small business owners what their costs are and they will name the obvious ones: stock, rent, maybe electricity. But when you sit down and list everything they actually spend money on, the number is always higher than they thought — sometimes twice as high.

This is not unusual. It is how most people think about costs. The problem is that if your costs are higher than you realise, your prices are probably too low, and you are slowly losing money while believing you are making money.

## Fixed Costs vs Variable Costs

**Fixed costs** are expenses that exist every month regardless of how much you sell. You pay them even on a day when you sell nothing.

Examples: shop rent, your own salary (yes, you deserve one), phone subscription, security fees, equipment loan repayments, association membership fees.

**Variable costs** are expenses that only occur when you are selling or producing something. They go up when you sell more and down when you sell less.

Examples: cost of goods/stock, packaging, delivery costs, ingredients for food preparation, commission to sales agents.

## The Hidden Costs Most Owners Forget

These are the costs that kill businesses quietly because nobody remembers to include them in pricing:

**Your own time.** You work 60 hours a week in your business. That time has value. Even if you pay yourself nothing, your time is a cost — if you were not running this business, you could be doing something else that earns money. Include at least a modest owner salary in your cost calculations.

**Transport.** The motorbike fuel to collect stock, the fare to the market and back, delivery to customers. These small trips add up to significant monthly amounts.

**Spoilage and waste.** If you sell food or perishable goods, not everything you buy gets sold. That unsold, spoiled portion is a cost that must be shared across everything you do sell.

**Equipment wear and maintenance.** Your fridge, your motorbike, your sewing machine — these break down and need repair. Dividing the average annual repair cost by 12 gives you a monthly cost to include.

**Bank charges and mobile money fees.** Every MTN Mobile Money or Orange Money transaction has a fee. For businesses doing many small transactions, this adds up to thousands of CFA monthly.

**Customer credit that goes unpaid.** Statistically, some percentage of credit given to customers will never be collected. A realistic loss rate of 5-10% on credit sales is a cost you should factor in.

## How to Calculate Your Break-Even Point

Your break-even point is the minimum amount you must sell in a month just to cover all your costs — before earning any profit at all.

Formula: **Break-even = Total Fixed Monthly Costs ÷ Gross Margin %**

Where Gross Margin % = (Selling Price - Variable Cost per unit) ÷ Selling Price

Example:
- Monthly fixed costs: 85,000 CFA (rent 50,000 + phone 5,000 + owner basic salary 30,000)
- You sell items at 1,000 CFA each that cost you 600 CFA each
- Gross margin per item: 400 CFA, margin % = 40%
- Break-even: 85,000 ÷ 0.40 = 212,500 CFA in monthly sales
- In units: 212,500 ÷ 1,000 = 213 items per month just to break even

If you are not selling 213 items per month, you are losing money even if every sale feels profitable.

## Action: The Cost Audit

This week, sit down and write every single thing you spend money on in a month. Include the ones you almost forgot. Add them up. Compare that number to what you thought your costs were. Then check your prices against that real number.

Most business owners who do this exercise find they need to either raise prices, reduce costs, or both. The ones who never do this exercise eventually wonder why their business is not growing despite constant hard work.

title: Basic Bookkeeping Without an Accountant
summary: You do not need to study accounting to keep proper records. These five simple habits will give you better financial visibility than most business owners twice your size.
author: BizNess Editorial
content:
# Basic Bookkeeping Without an Accountant

The word 'bookkeeping' makes many business owners anxious. It sounds like something that requires years of study, complex software, or a professional you cannot afford. None of that is true. Bookkeeping at its most basic is simply writing down what money comes in and what money goes out, every day, without missing anything.

That is it. The discipline of doing it consistently is what matters, not the complexity of how you do it.

## Why Records Matter — The Honest Truth

Without records, you are running your business blind. You cannot know whether you are actually profitable. You cannot identify which products make you the most money. You cannot spot a problem until it becomes a crisis. You cannot get a loan because no lender will trust your word alone about your business performance.

With records, even simple ones, you have evidence. You can see patterns. You can make decisions based on facts instead of feelings.

## The Five Things to Record Every Day

**1. Every sale.** Amount, what was sold, how it was paid (cash, mobile money, credit). Do not group them at the end of the day from memory — record each one as it happens or within the hour. Memory is unreliable under the pressure of a busy day.

**2. Every expense.** Every CFA that leaves your business for any reason. Stock purchases, transport, snacks you bought for the shop, airtime for business calls. If it is a business cost, record it.

**3. Credit given.** Every time you give goods or services without immediate payment, record: customer name, amount, date, and agreed repayment date.

**4. Credit received.** Every time you pay with cash on hand at the end of day, note the closing balance. This is your most basic cash flow check.

**5. Opening and closing cash.** Count your cash at the start of the day and again at closing. The difference, adjusted for sales and expenses, should balance. If it does not, something is missing — either unrecorded sales, unrecorded expenses, or a theft problem.

## The 10-Minute End-of-Day Routine

This routine, done consistently, will give you better financial clarity than most informal businesses in your area:

**Step 1 (3 minutes):** Record any sales you have not yet entered. Check mobile money transactions to capture anything you forgot.

**Step 2 (2 minutes):** Record any expenses from the day — receipts from your pocket, transport costs, anything you paid.

**Step 3 (2 minutes):** Count your cash. Compare to what you expect based on opening balance + sales - expenses. Note any difference.

**Step 4 (3 minutes):** Look at any customer credit activity — new credit given today, any payments received from existing debtors.

That is 10 minutes. Done every day, it gives you a complete picture of your business.

## The Monthly Review — 30 Minutes That Change Everything

At the end of each month, spend 30 minutes doing these four things:

- Add up total revenue for the month
- Add up total expenses for the month
- Calculate net profit (revenue - expenses)
- Compare to the previous month: are you growing, stable, or declining?

This simple monthly comparison is how you catch problems early. Revenue dropping two months in a row is a signal to investigate. Expenses rising without a corresponding revenue increase is a signal to cut costs.

## What About Tax?

Good records also protect you at tax time. If Cameroon's tax authority ever enquires about your business, records showing your real revenue and expenses are your best defence against arbitrary assessments. The impôt libératoire (flat-rate tax for small businesses) is calculated on estimated revenue — businesses with records can demonstrate their actual revenue and avoid being overcharged.

title: How to Get Financing for Your Business in Cameroon
summary: Banks are not the only option. Here is a complete guide to every financing path available to Cameroonian SME owners — from microfinance to government programs to tontines.
author: BizNess Editorial
content:
# How to Get Financing for Your Business in Cameroon

The number one complaint from Cameroonian SME owners is access to capital. Banks are difficult, interest rates are high, collateral requirements are impossible for most informal businesses. But bank loans are not the only option — and for most early-stage businesses, they are not even the best option.

This article maps every financing path available to you and explains honestly what each one requires.

## Option 1: The Tontine / Njangi

The most underrated financing tool in Cameroon. A tontine (called njangi in the Anglophone regions) is a rotating savings group where members contribute regularly and take turns receiving the full pot. For a business owner, receiving your turn is an interest-free lump sum that can be used to restock, buy equipment, or expand.

The advantage over a bank: no collateral, no paperwork, no interest, decision made by people who know you. The limitation: the amount is fixed by the group size and contribution level, and you must wait your turn.

If you are not already in a tontine, joining one — or forming one with fellow business owners — is the most practical first step toward access to capital.

## Option 2: Microfinance Institutions (MFIs)

Microfinance institutions exist specifically to serve clients who cannot access commercial banks. In Cameroon, major MFIs include CamCCUL (Cameroon Cooperative Credit Union League) and its affiliated credit unions across the country, MC2 (Mutuelles Communautaires de Croissance), and various CAMIF-affiliated cooperatives.

What they typically require:
- Membership in the institution (a small registration fee and savings deposit)
- A business with some operating history (typically 6-12 months)
- A basic business plan or at least a clear explanation of how the loan will be used
- Guarantors from within the community or co-signers
- In many cases, no hard collateral — your reputation and social guarantees are sufficient

Interest rates are higher than commercial banks but the accessibility is far greater.

## Option 3: Government Programs Through MINPMEESA

The Ministry of Small and Medium Enterprises (MINPMEESA) runs several support programs for SMEs including:

- **FAIJ (Fonds d'Aide à l'Insertion des Jeunes):** Targeted at young entrepreneurs under 35. Provides subsidised loans and business support services.
- **PAJER-U:** A youth employment and entrepreneurship program providing both training and access to financing.
- **Fonds de Garantie PME:** A guarantee fund that helps SMEs access bank loans by providing the bank with a government-backed guarantee.

These programs move slowly and have bureaucratic requirements, but the terms are far better than commercial alternatives. The CFCE offices can direct you to current programs available in your region.

## Option 4: Commercial Bank Loans

The hardest to access but the largest amounts. Cameroonian commercial banks (Afriland First Bank, SCB Cameroun, Ecobank, UBA, etc.) require:
- Formal business registration (RCCM number and NIU)
- Business bank account with transaction history
- Financial statements — at minimum 12 months of documented revenue and expenses
- Collateral (property, vehicle, or significant assets in most cases)
- A viable business plan for larger amounts

Without formal registration and documented financial history, a commercial bank loan is not accessible. This is one of the most practical reasons to formalise your business and keep proper records — you are building the evidence a bank needs.

## Option 5: Supplier Credit

Many business owners overlook this entirely. If you have a reliable relationship with a supplier, negotiate credit terms — pay 30 or 60 days after delivery instead of upfront. This is effectively free short-term financing. A supplier who trusts you will extend credit because they want your ongoing business.

Start building this relationship by paying consistently and on time for smaller transactions, then gradually negotiate terms for larger orders.

## Option 6: Customer Advance Payments

For service businesses and custom orders, requiring a 30-50% deposit before starting work is completely standard practice. This upfront payment finances your costs before you have completed the work. It is not unusual, it is not aggressive — it is normal business practice that protects both parties.

## What Every Lender Will Ask For

Regardless of which option you pursue, every lender wants to understand the same three things: Can you afford to repay? Will you be willing to repay? What happens if something goes wrong? Your financial records, your reputation, and your collateral (or lack of it) are your answers to those three questions. Building all three takes time — start now.

title: How to Get Your First 100 Customers
summary: Before you spend money on advertising, there are proven low-cost strategies that have built thousands of businesses in Cameroon. Here is what actually works.
author: BizNess Editorial
content:
# How to Get Your First 100 Customers

Most small business owners make the same mistake when thinking about customers: they think they need advertising. They want flyers, Facebook ads, a banner. Sometimes these work. More often, they are expensive and produce disappointing results.

The truth is that the first 100 customers of almost every successful business in Cameroon did not come from advertising. They came from something older and more powerful: trust, recommendation, and proximity.

## Strategy 1: Start Aggressively Within Your Network

Your first customers are people who already know you. Family, friends, former colleagues, neighbours, church members, association members, classmates. Every single one of these people is a potential customer or knows someone who is.

Do not be shy about this. Tell everyone you know what you are doing and what you sell. Be specific: not 'I have a business now' but 'I make fresh beignets every morning at the corner of Rue de la Paix from 6am — come and try, first order is on me.' Specificity gets remembered. Vagueness gets forgotten.

## Strategy 2: Make Your First Customers Your Salespeople

Every satisfied customer you have is more valuable than any advertisement you could buy. A recommendation from a trusted person converts at a far higher rate than a flyer handed to a stranger.

Actively ask your first customers for referrals. Not passively — actively. After serving them well: 'Do you have a colleague or neighbour who might also need this? I would appreciate the introduction very much.' Most people are happy to refer if you simply ask.

Offer a small incentive for referrals — a discount on their next purchase, a free addition to their order. This turns goodwill into action.

## Strategy 3: WhatsApp Business — Your Most Powerful Free Tool

WhatsApp Business is free, every potential customer already uses WhatsApp, and it reaches people directly in the same place they talk to family and friends. For a Cameroonian SME, it is more effective than any other marketing channel at low cost.

Set up a WhatsApp Business account with: a clear profile photo showing your products or business, your business name, hours, and location in the bio, and a catalogue of your products with photos and prices if you sell physical goods.

Broadcast a message to your contacts when you have new stock, a special offer, or simply to remind them you exist. Keep broadcasts relevant and not too frequent — once or twice a week is enough. Nobody wants to feel spammed.

## Strategy 4: Visibility in Physical Space

If your business operates from a physical location, people passing by are your most natural customers. Make your presence impossible to miss. A hand-painted sign is better than no sign. Samples placed where passing customers can see, smell, or touch them convert spectators into buyers.

For food businesses, the smell of cooking is your most powerful marketing tool. Position your cooking so the aroma reaches the street.

## Strategy 5: Price as a Growth Tool in the Beginning

In the early days, your goal is not maximum profit per transaction — it is maximum number of people who try your product and come back. Consider an introductory price slightly below what you will eventually charge, or a 'buy two get one' offer that encourages trial.

Be careful not to create a price expectation you cannot maintain. An introductory offer is fine if customers understand it is temporary. Raising prices later from a permanently low starting point is much harder than it seems.

## Strategy 6: Partnerships with Complementary Businesses

If you sell bread, who sells eggs nearby? If you do alterations, who sells fabric? Find businesses that serve the same customers as you but sell something different, and refer customers to each other. This costs nothing and multiplies your visibility through someone else's established customer base.

## The Consistency Principle

Most marketing for small businesses fails not because the strategy is wrong but because the owner gives up too early. Build the WhatsApp group, then go quiet after two weeks. Print the flyers, hand them out once, and wait. Distribute samples one time and declare the strategy useless when sales do not immediately explode.

Customers need to see you consistently over time before they trust you enough to buy. Show up every day, in the same place, with the same quality, at the same time. Consistency builds reputation. Reputation builds customers.

title: Surviving and Thriving Through Slow Seasons
summary: Every business has slow periods. The ones that survive them do not survive by accident — they prepare deliberately. Here is how to protect your business during low-sales months.
author: BizNess Editorial
content:
# Surviving and Thriving Through Slow Seasons

Every business in Cameroon has seasons. Food vendors see drops in January after the festive spending hangover. School supply shops empty out in February. Tailors are overwhelmed before Christmas and silent in February. Transport operators feel it during the rainy season. This is not a sign that something is wrong with your business — it is a predictable pattern that you can prepare for.

The businesses that fail during slow seasons are almost always the ones that treated the good season's money as income rather than survival buffer. The ones that survive are the ones that saw the slow season coming and prepared for it.

## Step 1: Identify Your Pattern

Before you can prepare for a slow season, you need to know when it comes and how severe it is. If you have been operating for at least one year, look at your records (or your memory) and answer: which two or three months are consistently your weakest? How much does revenue drop compared to your best months?

For most Cameroonian businesses, the post-Christmas period (January-February), the mid-rainy season (August-September), and sometimes the school-reopening period (September) when families have depleted savings are reliably challenging.

## Step 2: Build a Slow-Season Reserve During Good Months

This is the most important action and the one most people skip. During your strong months — before Christmas, before end-of-year — set aside a percentage of daily revenue specifically for slow season survival. Not for personal spending, not for expansion, specifically for keeping the business alive during the lean months.

A practical target: enough to cover your fixed costs (rent, utilities, your basic owner salary) for two to three months. For most small businesses this is between 150,000 and 500,000 CFA.

Keep this money separate from your operational funds — a different mobile money account, a second envelope, a savings account. Mixing it with operational funds means it will be spent without realising it.

## Step 3: Reduce Variable Costs During Slow Periods

When revenue drops, your fixed costs stay the same but your variable costs can be cut significantly. During a slow season:

- Reduce stock orders. Do not restock based on what you normally buy — restock based on what you are actually selling now.
- Reduce staff hours if you have part-time workers.
- Defer non-essential maintenance to the next good season.
- Negotiate with suppliers for smaller, more frequent orders rather than large lump-sum orders.

The danger is cutting too deep and having nothing to sell when demand returns. Keep a minimum viable stock level — enough to serve customers who do come, not enough to sit unsold.

## Step 4: Generate Income From Your Slow Season

Some businesses successfully use their slow season to diversify income temporarily. A tailor who has no Christmas order rush in February might take on school uniform repairs. A food vendor who sees lower lunch traffic might pivot to evening catering for nearby offices or events. A hardware shop owner might offer delivery services in their slow months.

These are not permanent changes to your business model — they are tactical moves to cover costs during a predictable difficult period.

## Step 5: Use the Slow Season Productively

The slow season is actually a gift that the good season never gives you: time. Use it deliberately.

- Deep-clean and reorganise your shop or workspace
- Review your pricing structure and update it before the next busy season
- Call customers you have not seen in a while and check in with them
- Learn something new — a skill, a language, a better process
- Prepare your stock and pricing strategy for the upcoming busy season so you are ready when it arrives

Businesses that invest their slow-season time in preparation consistently outperform their competitors when the busy season returns.

title: When and How to Hire Your First Employee
summary: Hiring too early destroys cash flow. Hiring too late destroys growth. Here is how to know when the time is right and how to do it properly in Cameroon.
author: BizNess Editorial
content:
# When and How to Hire Your First Employee

The moment you hire your first employee, your business changes permanently. You go from being a person who runs a business to being an employer with legal responsibilities, people management obligations, and a fixed cost that exists whether your revenue is strong or not.

That is not a reason to avoid hiring — it is a reason to hire thoughtfully.

## The Three Signals That Tell You It Is Time

**Signal 1: You are consistently turning away or delaying work.**
If customers are waiting too long, if you are saying no to orders because you cannot fulfill them, if you are regularly working past 10pm just to keep up — your capacity is the constraint on your revenue. An employee would directly increase what you can earn.

**Signal 2: The revenue is there and stable, not just in a good week.**
Do not hire on the basis of one exceptional month. Look at your last three to six months. Is revenue consistently above your break-even by enough to cover an employee's salary and all the associated costs? The key word is consistently. One good month followed by a weak one is not a stable foundation for a new hire.

**Signal 3: You are spending time on things that could be done by someone less expensive.**
If you — the founder, the strategist, the relationship-builder — are spending four hours a day on delivery runs or packaging or cleaning, you are using your most valuable hours on your least valuable tasks. An employee at a fraction of your effective hourly rate could do those things, freeing you to do things that generate more revenue.

## The True Cost of an Employee

This is where many first-time employers get surprised. An employee does not cost only their salary.

In Cameroon, when you formally employ someone, the legal costs include:

- **Gross salary** (what you have agreed to pay)
- **CNPS employer contribution** — approximately 11.2% of gross salary for accident insurance, family benefits, and old-age pension contributions
- **IRPP** (income tax on salaries) — withheld from the employee and paid to the tax authority, adding administrative burden

So a formal employee earning a net salary of 50,000 CFA per month actually costs you approximately 60,000 to 65,000 CFA when all obligations are included.

Additionally factor in: training time (productivity is lower for the first 1-3 months), management time (you will spend time directing and reviewing their work), potential mistakes and their costs, and tools or equipment they need.

A realistic rule: budget 1.3 to 1.5 times the nominal salary as the true monthly cost of a formal employee.

## The Minimum Wage

Cameroon's SMIG (Salaire Minimum Interprofessionnel Garanti) is the legally required minimum monthly salary. As of the most recent revision, this stands at 41,875 CFA per month. Paying below this is illegal regardless of any agreement with the employee.

## Formal vs Informal Employment

Many SME owners employ people informally — a daily worker paid in cash, a helper with no contract. This is common but carries real risk: if the worker is injured on the job, you are personally liable. If they claim employment rights they are legally entitled to, you have no paperwork protecting you. If you apply for a bank loan or government contract, undeclared workers can become a problem.

Formal employment through CNPS registration is not as complex as feared. The CNPS office can guide you through registration and the process is straightforward once you have your NIU.

## Writing a Simple Employment Agreement

Even for an informal or part-time arrangement, a written agreement protects both parties. It should state: the job title and responsibilities, the salary and payment schedule, working hours and days, the probation period (typically one to three months), and notice period required by either side to end the arrangement.

This does not need a lawyer for a basic role. A clearly written one-page document signed by both parties and witnessed by a third party is effective and enforceable.

## The First 90 Days

Most hiring failures happen because the employer assumed the new person would figure everything out without guidance. Be explicit about what you expect, how you measure good performance, and what a successful first month looks like. Check in weekly. Correct problems early before bad habits set in. And if after 90 days the person is clearly not working out, end it cleanly and professionally. A bad hire kept too long is more damaging than the difficulty of replacing them.
